records.title: Show HN: KiviDB, a faster Redis-compatible memory database and vector cache
records.author: murtazayusuf
records.storyText:
Hi all,

So I have been working on this project KiviDB from February 2026. It started as a project for me to understand rust, having a product with no GC pauses, memory blow up after snapshots and getting OOM on running pods, and that was actually an issue I faced with Dragonfly. I wanted to have something picking the best of Rust, but also picking the best parts of other alternatives like Garnet and Dragonfly. I used AI a lot, but I was the one making the design decisions based on the tests that claude picked from my history of troubleshooting sessions as part of my job. KiviDB supports both RESP2 and RESP3 protocol. I had some founders credits on my AWS account which helped me with the infra, and running instances I could perform benchmark on.

Its keyspace is sharded across threads, it is multi-threaded in nature, and performs best on Linux due to io_uring, I used the tokio_uring crate for this. It also has tokio fallback for other OS's. I hadn't open sourced it until recently as I felt it was not ready yet, the best way to learn it was to build a cloud managed service for it across all three widely used cloud providers i.e AWS, GCP and azure. Since I used to mainly work with cloud, I had some insights on what would be the best ways for the deployments, how to conduct failovers, manage SLAs, etc. And that's what I took help from claude to fast pace it. The website does look like AI slop but it works for now, given my limited resources, that's all I had. You may check it out at : https://kividb.io, I open sourced the core engine under AGPLv3, didn't want to have just source available, because that is available with other tools too. It supports apprx 98-99% of the redis 8.10 commands, few have issues and you can find them at https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/issues, contributors are welcome.

Now the numbers, for the final benchmark, I used 2 c7gn.metal servers, in the same placement group in us-east1, and I used memtier-benchmark tool for this. The setting was : 10M keys, 100B each, 32 cores in use with both pipeline and un-pipelined runs.

pipeline 16 GET: KiviDB 21.2M ops/sec vs Dragonfly 2.0 9.1M, Redis 8.10 2.4M, Redis Cluster 32 shards 4.7M

When not pipelined, Dragonfly performed slightly better at 3.35M ops/sec vs kividb at 3.07M ops/sec. Memory per key was also slightly worse than dragonfly and almost same as Redis, 177B (kividb) vs 134B (dragonfly) vs 178B (redis).

With vector ingestion times it was slower but when querying, it was faster than most alternatives at lower ef, however slower than dragonfly at high ef. Most of the technical details are mentioned here so you can check it out: https://kividb.io/benchmarks.

easiest way to try it: docker run -d -p 6380:6380 kividb/kividb

I am looking forward to building a community around this, provide better rust based tools, I am open to constructive criticism and value informed opinion. Thanks

records.title: Show HN: I built a task system to handle the drudgery so I could focus on tasks
records.author: dmayle
records.storyText:
I'm a software engineer from the east coast (who has lived in Boston, NY, the bay area, UK, France), and I built a task system called 3 & Done. It's the place you trust to store everything you need to do. It accepts voice input for rapid entry, as well as text (it stores the audio locally so you can listen to jog your memory) and emails you every morning with the three most important things for you to do that day, and why, based on what you've said about the task: deadlines, urgency, sitting too long.

I've been at software engineering for about 44 years now... Grew up with it, which was unusual when I started, and I was always good about getting into the zone and doing things. The career started small, small company, then back office, the dot com startups, then smaller companies again after the bust, a non-profit, and eventually YouTube (Google at the time, but just barely) and Meta (just Facebook when I was there).

When I hit the startups, and later big tech, it was no longer enough to just be an engineer, to have drive, to be good, you had to be organized, you had to follow through, get stuff done, and that's where the task systems started. Twenty-five over the years (and yes, I've actually counted), from Moleskine notebooks with Getting Things Done, evernote (remember evernote?), bug trackers, todoist, asana, google keep, among others.

When I managed on the Facebook News Feed, I got into gantt charts (for me and my team), spreadsheets, OmniPlan... I remember apologizing to my director for being so disorganized (because I felt I was making a mess of it), and he told me that I was the most organized engineer he knew.

That was because I was doing all of the work in the background, the trimming, the sorting, the reviews, but it was just so much work. Which was why I changed from system to system. Each time it built up, and I had to spend more time looking at things I couldn't or didn't get done, when I was rushed and couldn't put time into today's review, it would pile up, and then using it was so much work that I would start taking mini-notes, just emailing myself a few things to do the next day.

That's actually the thesis of the app (but not where it started), that if I could just have a few things to do emailed to me each day, I could get it done.

This app actually started when I described my previous startup failures into a Claude web session, and it repeated back to me what I had just said. My previous failures were because I spent too much time building the stuff I needed, and not building what I was supposed to be building.

I decided that the app would email me three things to do every day (which matches best practices for attention), but that the day was always yours to decide. We won't overload you, but you can add more, if you're feeling up to it, or cut back, and we never shame and try our best not to nag (I often only finish two). If we get it wrong, you can tell us, and we'll re-rank it once a day, or you can set it manually, and if you do, we never override that choice. The web app is live, and native for both platforms is coming. In the meantime, on Android, you can use gestures to quick launch into the voice input so saving a task is only a gesture away (e.g. double-tap the back of a Pixel, double-press the power button on Motorola).

Now let's talk about the dirty parts. I used AI to help me build this. Anthropic models mostly, and the brains of the app come from Anthropic models (I like the quality, I like the privacy, absolutely no training on customer data, and the stance of the company). This app is not some one-shot wonder where I asked frontier models to build a task system and then I put it on a server to show you.

I have prompts for the various features (e.g. ranking, generating suggestions, task extractions), I have eval sets of task lists (not anyone's real tasks, but constructed from patterns in my tasks, or the tasks of testers who allowed me to fix the problems they were having), with the three I expect to come out. I store the eval outputs, and re-test whenever I add a new rule to a prompt, or whenever testing a new model version. The great thing about having this eval set is that it catches when I get it wrong. When I introspect a failed run, sometimes it's because I need to tune a prompt, but sometimes it's because I missed something in my own ranking.

I did the same thing with my infrastructure as well, so this time, instead of setting up servers, and building login systems, and managing databases, I built on Vercel (git push to serving Next.js), Neon (hosted postgres).

I started getting emails mailed to me by mid-June, but started getting usable suggestions on June 26, and I've been using it every morning since. I wanted it to be easy to get started, and easy to use, so the input handles mess (you can add multiple tasks in the same run-on sentence, and a friend who helped me test it just pasted his entire obsidian todo list in wholesale to get started).

I wanted to make sure that anyone could try it out, so I built a trial feature that uses the real in-app ranking with a list of items you provide.

If you want to try the service, there's a free 14-day trial (card required), and then it's $99/year or $9.99/month after that (plus sales tax). We warn you seven days before your card is charged and if you cancel, you keep access through the term (either the trial, or our last paid period). Online, through settings -> billing, no email, no call.

I really hope you'll try it out. If you do, please tell me if we did a good job picking out your day.

https://3anddoneapp.com/try

records.title: Show HN: Pi-cowboy – use Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode as subagents
records.author: suoloordi
records.storyText:
pi-cowboy is an agent orchestrator for Pi(https://pi.dev) and Herdr(https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr). Break large jobs into focused subtasks, hand them off to background agents running in parallel, and consolidate the results when they finish. Each agent runs in an isolated copy-on-write Git work-tree, minimising disk overhead.

pi-cowboy can orchestrate foreign harnesses too, including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and more.

Feature highlights:

- Foreign harnesses: pi-cowboy agents can run in Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pig and Pi-Bolt, as well as Pi. This gives you great flexibility in choosing how to spend your tokens. Running out of Codex usage? Switch your pi-cowboy harness to OpenCode, select one of its free models, and let it handle the rest. Pig and Pi-Bolt are pi variants that are more efficient, with a lower memory footprint and faster performance than pi. Because pi-cowboy is designed to run multiple agents in parallel, having a lower per-agent footprint is crucial. It prevents your machine from running out of resources and lets you have higher concurrency without choking your system.

- Concurrency limits: You can configure concurrency limits at every level. Running a local model with limited resources? If a simple task already takes hours to complete, the last thing you want is to overload your machine by running too many of them at once. Set concurrency limits for that model specifically to keep resource usage under control.

You can install it on Pi as a package:

  pi install npm:pi-cowboy #(requires `herdr` 0.8+)

records.title: Show HN: Correct Hooks – Easy webhook auth with asymmetric signatures
records.author: pdiffles
records.storyText:
A while back, I needed to make a webhook system for a project I was working on. I pretty quickly found out that webhook auth is not an entirely solved problem with people frequently implementing DIY solutions. I also found out that while using some form of asymmetric signature (eg. oauth tokens) is common with regular api auth, most webhook producers use symmetric signatures (HMAC) instead.

This bugged the hell out of me because the webhook functionality I needed was pretty basic, but using symmetric signatures, which requires the webhook producer to hold onto a secret for every endpoint they send webhooks to, introduced a major secret management problem. Designing and implementing novel secret management techniques for my web app felt like a bad idea, so I started looking into why so many people use symmetric signatures instead of asymmetric signatures.

I frequently saw performance listed as a problem with asymmetric signatures, so I thought this might be why they weren't more broadly used, but a quick benchmark proved that wrong (HMAC signing is much faster, but ed25519 is still fast enough that it doesn't matter).

It seemed like the biggest barrier to using asymmetric signatures was added development complexity. There are small but important details that need to be included in an asymmetric signature, getting asymmetric keys into the right format is more complicated than for symmetric keys, and the crypto libraries you're working with can have sharp edges.

That complexity makes it more difficult for a webhook producer to implement (and document) asymmetric signatures, but then all of their consumers also have to implement the verification step (hopefully correctly). Building a library that does these steps for you is difficult because it has to be available in any language a webhook consumer might be using, not just the language the webhook producer uses.

But it kept bugging me that we're all using a less good form of authentication just because we haven't packaged up the steps to sign and verify an asymmetric signature that is secure for webhooks, so now I've built that library. With a few language implementations to serve as a template, replicating this in enough languages that the large majority of developers can use it feels totally doable, and I am hoping to get several more languages implemented over the next few weeks.

records.title: Show HN: Chest – a tiny, open-source menu bar manager for macOS 27
records.author: a-ve
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

One of my favorite apps on macOS, Ice, stopped working when I updated to macOS 27 because the trick it relied on doesn't work anymore. The only thing I really needed from the app was the ability to hide menu bar items to the left of it, so I built Chest to do just that.

There are other apps like this as well that try to use the menu bar part of macOS's exam mode to hide items, but that approach has some issues with the screen sharing, microphone, and camera indicators in the menu bar, which is rather troublesome for me.

Chest works by emulating the "Allow in the Menu Bar" switches in System Settings rather than relying on the old trick of pushing menu bar items off-screen.

It just needs Accessibility permission and access to two files that let it control which items are shown in the menu bar and where they're placed.

You can hide items in two ways: by ⌘-dragging them to the left of a small dot in the menu bar, or by dropping them into a separate "Chest" that keeps them out of the menu bar entirely. Clicking the dot brings the hidden items back.

I think our approach is rather cleaner, and the app itself sits at ~2 MB, so it's small enough to not matter while providing a clutter-free menu bar.

You can view the source at https://github.com/boringbar/chest

records.title: Show HN: Reversing Wing Commander to find the entity table in 64k to add co-op
records.author: daniel_rh
records.storyText:
I've always wanted to play Wing Commander with friends, so we could fly the story missions together. In 2015, I hypothesized that the full game state fit in the data segment (only 64k), and I could do small position and orientation experiments with vbindiff to discover how the memory was organized. Some fun findings: the camera was in entity index 0x3D (a "3D" joke?). My brother, Patrick, figured out Borland's overlay loader crashed the game until we made our stub look like a real stack frame. To play you need your own copy (e.g. the GOG version) and you drag setup.exe into the browser. It's a DOSBox mod: no game files are hosted. We reversed the game by hand, but LLMs were used for the recent browser/peer-to-peer WebRTC with voice chat port recently, and we continue to use them for ongoing work.

I'll be in the lobby for some hours if anyone wants to fly together.

records.title: Show HN: Firmendaten: Parsed balance sheets for every Austrian company
records.author: leo_researchly
records.storyText:
Ever since January 2025 the Austrian Ministry of Justice has made the Firmenbuch public (and free!) as part of the EUs Open Data Directive.

Firmendaten builds on that: we ingest the filings, extract the balance sheet figures (which, luckily, mostly come as an XML), and make them searchable and comparable across companies and years.

When we set out to do it, it sounded pretty easy: extract the XML, save them in a table, calculate the KPIs and build the from-tend.

However, a few things made it harder than expected.

- Fiscal years don't line up. We compare the latest year both companies filed for. If there is none, each column shows its own latest year and is labelled as such. We also only match on the year, so a balance sheet dated 31 March and one dated 31 December both count as "2024". There's quite some (internal) discussion on how to handle that.

- Small companies don't have to disclose revenue. Small GmbHs/FlexCos file an abridged balance sheet without a P&L, so margins simply aren't available for a large share of companies. Our "growth" figure falls back to total assets, which is a weak signal: it also grows when a company takes on debt. On a more general note: not every financial figure makes equal sense for every industry / company. Ideally, we would have specific numbers, based on the industry.

- Holding companies break ratios. They book dividends from subsidiaries as income on almost no revenue, which gives you profit margins above 100%. That's actually just one part of the issue around holding companies, and subsidies.

- Generated summaries overclaim easily. "Company A is more stably financed" really just means "higher equity ratio". We're still tuning the wording, which is one reason the page is labelled beta. None of the summaries are AI-generated, as that requires quite some tweaking to get right (agin, a lot of the interpretation depends on the industry/company).

records.title: Show HN: Hypereffect, a hypermedia protocol that renders reactive UIs everywhere
records.author: andunie
records.storyText:
The idea is that whenever you have a server (which can be a remote server, but also just another process in the same machine, or even a sandboxed WASM module running in the same process as the renderer) they can send some simple messages and those can be turned into an interactive and reactive UI.

The renderer can be running in a terminal, a native app or basically anywhere else.

I guess it's somewhat like HTML, but purposefully much simpler so it can be implemented very easily, with built-in reactivity, no arbitrary code execution and a very limited set of components, so the server (mostly) can't influence _how_ things look on the client, only _what_.

records.title: Show HN: Acyclic; Rapid agent swarms
records.author: ramstar3000
records.storyText:
Hi HN, we're the co-founders of Acyclic (YC F26).

Acyclic runs any agentic workflow as a swarm. You give it a task and your project; it splits the work across many coding agents, each in its own sandbox, runs them in parallel, and merges what they produce into one patch or pull request.

Our thesis: agentic workflows should be realtime, no matter how complex the task. The bottleneck should be human ideation and design, whilst building happens at the speed of thought.

To bring this to you we make our agents recursively fork and speculative execute. This means that if an agent has 2 independent tasks to do, it will just split into 2 agents to solve both tasks quickly and merge back up the tree. Additionally, for sequential operations we have “speculative” agents which guess the next steps of the workflow as a pre-fetch step.

To make this efficient we are solving the infrastructure bottlenecks. We are solving the memory, communication, routing and durable execution issues. This infra is open source at acyclic.dev/github, so check it out!

To run your own swarm (check out acyclic.dev for a full guide)

``` npm install -g @acyclic-labs/cli acyclic swarm run --task <prompt> --dir <files_to_upload> ```

A good (non-coding) first task to try out: Do deep research into a person. “Do deep research into Jeff Goldblum“ You can view the results at acyclic.dev/dashboard or stream the results back to the cli using:

``` acyclic swarm pull <swarm-id> --apply ```

Check out some more research examples at acyclic.dev/evals, right now our biggest useful swarm is 236 agents for a code migration.

records.title: Show HN: WeDecide – A tool for easier decision making for group trips
records.author: utorious_big
records.storyText:
Hey!

In my spare time I am working on this little tool to let groups vote on accomodation/budget/dates for trips.

I started building it, because the yearly trip with our friends got out of hand before it even started. After a lot of back and forth we were able to decide on date and budget, but the accomodation itself turned out to be a stress test for our friendships. From time to time new links got thrown into the group chat, in between all other messages. In the end we decided for a rather random accomodation, nobody was really happy with.

While our trip in the end turned out to be great - with the right people the accomodation does not matter much - I was convinced a little app could benefit us and maybe others aswell. So I started building WeDecide.

I wanted to achieve the following:

* The focus is on the decision making, not on research.

* It should work in combination with a group chat, not be an all in one tool.

* Everyone in the chat should be easily involved. That means simple UX and no registration. I had doodle in mind for this.

To finance it the app generates affiliate links of a number of hotel platforms. I won't get rich of it!

Some technical details: It's a Nuxt app + postgres db running on a 5€ per month server of a german provider. Additionally I set up Bunny CDN. Tracking is done via a self hosted Plausible instance. Everything is hosted in Europe by European companies.

Feedback is very much welcome and hopefully this tool is useful for somebody!

Cheers

records.title: Show HN: ApolloOffice – Local AI workers that turn GitHub issues into tested PRs
records.author: NetterSilver
records.storyText:
This is a little thing I built: it's a visually pleasing office with AI agents working on GitHub repositories and submitting pull requests. They are getting issues, reproduce them and then fix them. I was using it privately in a Discord call and many people requested a public open-source version, so I got Claude Opus 5.5 to rewrite the entire code in Rust. It's available as a service on macOS, Linux and Windows.

In my use case I use it to make PRs for ArtCraft, the Adobe Suite clone that is viral right now. This tool got me into the top 10 contributors within 5 days. I have 361 total pull requests, 234 of them got merged. I think that statistic speaks for the quality this thing can achieve. Right now on low usage settings it's round about 51 pulls a day fast, and it does not use up as much usage as you think it would, mainly because the tasks get split between Haiku models on default settings and not everything is running on one big Opus session. Also they get optimal prompts and clear instructions every step, which further reduces token usage. It can also bughunt: about 60% of pulls are code problems the tool found by itself.

If you are a GitHub contributor to any project or want to solve issues on your own repository, this is the tool for you.

records.title: Show HN: I recreated Contra in a custom NES game engine (NOT an emulator)
records.author: normalocity
records.storyText:
Here's a demo video I recorded for a friend that I decided to repost. Sorry for the terrible sound quality and my cough -- hope it's mostly understandable.

https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/jeffluntgames.com/the-sur...

---

Here's the technical breakdown of what I did:

* Worked with an AI agent (of course) * Described the basic features of the NES * Sprite engine * Input handling * Sound and music

Had the AI build what I'll call a microengine around this. Why do I call it a microengine? Because games on the NES were, I assume, written in assembly, without game engines. But my micro engine (which I named `neo8`) looks like a high-level language, has a basic camera system, and event-based sound system, a polling and event-based input handler that maps inputs to in-game events, a way to model game entities (entity attributes, rendering, animation state machines, etc.), but really just the very basics of what you'd need to create NES-style games on modern hardware.

To be clear, `neo8` is _not_ an emulator. It cannot run NES ROMs. But part of the engine, for the purpose of this demo, involved creating an image, audio, and code structure analysis tool so that I could convert the raw binary data from an actual ROM into .png files, mp3 files, and high-level code.

That high-level code is then compiled to a zero-dependency, native binary, and the little engine supports win/mac/linux as binary outputs.

Anyway, it was fun. Why not just port Contra directly (the "reverse engineer anything" repo, I'm sure could do it direct from the ROM to Rust or something). But I didn't want Contra, because I could just play the real Contra on original hardware or an emulator. Recreating Contra wasn't the point.

The point was to create the engine so I could create new, cross-platform NES-style games using a tiny engine. The Contra demo was simply a proof-of-concept to see if my little engine could replicate Contra's gameplay style, and sure enough it pretty much worked.
